Checked integer conversion
==========================

Import Narrowing.module's Checked theory and write:

  (try-narrow uint64_t uint32_t (post++ value) destination)

The first two fields are compact declaration specifiers. The input expression
must have the first type; the destination must be an addressable modifiable
object of the second type. The GNU profile supports the integral types admitted
by the native __builtin_add_overflow primitive. Floating types, bit-fields and
const destinations are refused. Additional restrictions on integer extensions
follow the selected compiler's builtin contract.

Evaluation order is input first, then the destination's address, each once.
These argument effects occur even when conversion fails. On success the macro
stores the exact integer and returns int 1. On failure it leaves the destination
unchanged and returns int 0. The macro introduces no return, break, continue or
goto. It can be nested in ordinary C expression contexts.

The overflow primitive computes value + 0 at unbounded integer precision and
checks whether the destination type can represent that integer. Its temporary
conversion result is copied to the caller's destination only on success.
CompilerBuiltin/CompilerRef denotes this native primitive explicitly; a C
preprocessor definition of its name is refused at import and expansion points.

This contract uses ordinary C object validity and pointer access requirements.
A null or otherwise invalid destination is not an admitted addressable object.
An opaque native fragment cannot be a typed macro argument.

Native tests cover signed/unsigned boundaries, wide-to-small conversion,
failure preservation, evaluation order, type/category refusals, native export
and identical objects against independent handwritten C at O0 and O2.
MacroCheckedNarrowing proves the corresponding integer-range/store contract
against independent accept/below/above rules. The builtin's native implementation
and its lowering from the shipped template are tested, not proved by that law.
